slides.text: When I decided to finally renovate my historic home, I found a loose floorboard in the attic hiding a stack of fifty unmailed letters. They were written in 1960 by a man named Arthur, to a woman named Clara. They were the most intensely romantic, desperate love letters I had ever read. He begged her to meet him at the pier to run away, but apparently, he never found the courage to send them.

Obsessed with the tragic romance, I tracked down Arthur's family. I found his grandson, Henry, a quiet historian with warm hazel eyes and a surprisingly gentle smile. We met at a coffee shop so I could return the letters. As we read through them together, crying and laughing over his grandfather's poetic, heartbreaking drama, our coffees completely went cold. We ended up talking until the cafe closed.

We spent the next six months completely inseparable. On a rainy Tuesday, Henry brought me to the very pier his grandfather had written about. He pulled a new, slightly crumpled envelope from his coat pocket. 'My grandfather never mailed his letters because he was terrified of being rejected,' Henry whispered, his hands shaking as he handed it to me. 'I'm not making his mistake.' Inside, it simply read: 'Marry me.'
